questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a cellulose molecule. (2)
hints: Which isomer of glucose is it made from?
Think about how neighbouring chains are held together.
questions.solution:
Made of β-glucose (monomers) [B1]
Joined by 1-4 glycosidic bonds (alternate monomers inverted) [B1]
Straight / unbranched chains [B1]
Chains linked by hydrogen bonds to form microfibrils. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Cellulose is a polymer of β-glucose joined by 1-4 glycosidic bonds, with alternate monomers inverted, giving long straight unbranched chains held together by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils. (Any 2 points.)

questions.prompt: Starch is made of two polysaccharides, amylose and amylopectin. Describe the structure of starch. (2)
hints: Both are made from the same monomer.
Which one is branched?
questions.solution:
Polymer of α-glucose [B1]
Amylose: 1-4 glycosidic bonds, unbranched (helical) [B1]
Amylopectin: 1-4 and 1-6 glycosidic bonds, so branched. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Starch is a polymer of α-glucose. Amylose has only 1-4 glycosidic bonds and coils into an unbranched helix; amylopectin has 1-4 and 1-6 bonds, so it is branched. (Any 2 points.)

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which the structure of glycogen makes it suitable as an energy store in animal cells. (2)
hints: Think about how quickly glucose needs to be released.
Think about its effect on water potential.
questions.solution:
Highly branched, so many ends for (rapid) hydrolysis / enzyme action [B1]
Insoluble, so does not affect water potential / osmosis [B1]
Compact, so a lot stored in a small space [B1]
Large molecule, so cannot leave the cell. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two explained features, e.g. it is highly branched so there are many ends for enzymes to hydrolyse quickly; it is insoluble so it doesn't change the cell's water potential.

questions.prompt:
Which equation represents the formation of a dipeptide?

Choose one answer.

A  dipeptide + water → amino acid + amino acid
B  amino acid + amino acid + water → dipeptide
C  amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water
D  amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + ATP (1)
hints: Is a dipeptide formed by condensation or hydrolysis?
Which side of the equation is water on?
questions.solution:
C [B1]

Model answer:
C: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water (a condensation reaction).

questions.prompt:
An enzyme was incubated with excess substrate at 30 °C and at 60 °C. The graph shows the mass of product formed over time.

Explain the shapes of both curves. (4)
hints: Compare the initial rates first — what does temperature do to kinetic energy?
Why does the 60 °C curve level off at a lower mass of product?
questions.solution:
At 60 °C, faster initial rate because more kinetic energy, so more enzyme–substrate complexes formed [B1]
At 60 °C, enzyme denatured (over time) — hydrogen / ionic bonds broken, changing the tertiary structure [B1]
Active site changes shape so substrate no longer fits / is not complementary, so no more product formed (curve levels off) [B1]
At 30 °C, slower rate but enzyme not denatured, so product keeps increasing (reaches a higher total). [B1]

questions.prompt:
The graph shows the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of an enzyme.

Explain why the rate of reaction is low at pH 2 and at pH 12. (4)
hints: What do H⁺ and OH⁻ ions affect in a protein?
Link the change in structure to enzyme–substrate complexes.
questions.solution:
Concentration of H⁺ / OH⁻ ions changes [B1]
Breaks ionic / hydrogen bonds (in the tertiary structure) [B1]
Active site changes shape / substrate no longer complementary [B1]
Fewer enzyme–substrate complexes formed. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The graph shows the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction at different substrate concentrations, with and without an inhibitor.

Explain the results shown in the graph. (4)
hints: At high substrate concentration the two curves almost meet — what type of inhibitor does that suggest?
Why does the curve without inhibitor level off?
questions.solution:
Inhibitor is competitive / similar shape to substrate, so binds to the active site [B1]
At low substrate concentration, inhibitor occupies active sites, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes / lower rate [B1]
At high substrate concentration, substrate outcompetes inhibitor, so rate approaches the same maximum [B1]
Without inhibitor, rate levels off because all active sites are occupied / enzyme concentration is limiting. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug inhibits an enzyme in a malaria parasite but does not inhibit the human enzyme that catalyses the same reaction. Suggest why. (1)
hints: Same reaction does not mean same protein.
Link primary structure to shape.
questions.solution: Different amino acid sequence / primary structure, so different tertiary structure / shape of binding site, so drug not complementary. [B1]

questions.prompt: An RNA nucleotide contains a phosphate group. Name the other two components of an RNA nucleotide. (1)
hints: Compare with a DNA nucleotide: one component is different.
One component is a pentose sugar.
questions.solution: Ribose and a (nitrogenous / organic) base (both needed); accept a named base A, U, C or G. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which equation represents the hydrolysis of ATP?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ
B  ADP + Pᵢ → ATP + H₂O
C  ATP → ADP + Pᵢ + H₂O
D  ATP + H₂O → AMP + Pᵢ (1)
hints: Hydrolysis uses water as a reactant.
One phosphate is removed.
questions.solution:
A [B1]

Model answer:
A: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ (hydrolysis uses water and removes one phosphate).

questions.prompt:
Which statement about ATP is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP contains deoxyribose
B  ATP synthase catalyses condensation of ADP and Pᵢ
C  ATP hydrolase joins ADP and Pᵢ
D  ATP is a long-term energy store (1)
hints: Think about how ATP is made in the light-dependent reaction and respiration.
Which enzyme makes ATP?
questions.solution:
B [B1]

Model answer:
B: ATP synthase catalyses a condensation reaction between ADP and Pᵢ.

questions.prompt: Other than the nucleus, name the two organelles in a plant cell that contain their own DNA. (1)
hints: Think about which organelles are thought to have evolved from free-living prokaryotes.
One of them is the site of aerobic respiration.
questions.solution: Mitochondria and chloroplasts (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Penicillin prevents bacteria forming cell walls. Suggest why penicillin does not harm human cells. (1)
hints: What structure does a human cell lack?
What are bacterial cell walls made of?
questions.solution: Human cells do not have a cell wall / murein (peptidoglycan). [B1]

questions.prompt: An antibiotic binds to bacterial 70S ribosomes and stops translation. Suggest why it does not stop translation in the cytoplasm of human cells. (1)
hints: Are human cytoplasmic ribosomes the same size as bacterial ones?
Binding depends on shape.
questions.solution: Human (cytoplasmic) ribosomes are 80S / larger / a different shape, so the antibiotic does not bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast the structure of prokaryotic cells with the structure of eukaryotic cells. (6)
hints: Give paired differences: prokaryotes have … whereas eukaryotes have …
Think about DNA, organelles, ribosomes and the cell wall.
questions.solution:
Prokaryotes have no nucleus — DNA free in cytoplasm; eukaryotes have a nucleus [B1]
Prokaryotic DNA circular; eukaryotic DNA linear [B1]
Prokaryotic DNA not associated with histones; eukaryotic DNA is [B1]
Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles (e.g. mitochondria); eukaryotes do [B1]
Prokaryotes have smaller (70S) ribosomes; eukaryotes have larger (80S) ribosomes [B1]
Prokaryotic cell wall made of murein / peptidoglycan; plant / fungal walls made of cellulose / chitin [B1]
Prokaryotes may have plasmids / capsule / flagella of different structure [B1]
Prokaryotic cells are smaller. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

Model answer:
Any 6 contrasting points (each must state both sides).

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and the transmission electron microscope (TEM). (6)
hints: Give similarities first, then differences.
Where does the electron beam go in each one?
questions.solution:
Similarity: both use a beam of electrons (focused by electromagnets) [B1]
Similarity: both need a vacuum, so specimens must be dead [B1]
Similarity: both have higher resolution than optical microscopes / produce black-and-white images [B1]
TEM: electrons pass through the specimen; SEM: electrons are scattered / bounce off the surface [B1]
TEM gives 2D images of internal structure; SEM gives 3D images of surfaces [B1]
TEM has higher resolution (about 0.1 nm) than SEM [B1]
TEM specimens must be extremely thin; SEM specimens need not be [B1]
Both may show artefacts from preparation. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

Model answer:
Any 6 points; at least one similarity and one difference.

questions.prompt: Describe how cell fractionation and ultracentrifugation can be used to obtain a sample of mitochondria from liver tissue. Explain the conditions used. (6)
hints: Explain why the solution is cold, isotonic and buffered.
Which organelle forms the first pellet?
questions.solution:
Cold — reduces enzyme activity / stops organelles being digested [B1]
Isotonic — prevents osmosis, so organelles do not burst or shrink [B1]
Buffered — keeps pH constant so proteins / enzymes are not denatured [B1]
Homogenise (blend) tissue, then filter to remove debris / whole cells [B1]
Centrifuge at low speed; nuclei form the first pellet [B1]
Spin supernatant at a higher speed; mitochondria form the next pellet. [B1]

Model answer:
6 points.

questions.prompt: Viruses are not cells and cannot divide. Describe how a virus is replicated. (2)
hints: Viruses need a host cell.
What does the virus put into the host cell?
questions.solution:
Attachment proteins bind to (complementary) receptors on the host cell [B1]
Viral nucleic acid (DNA / RNA) enters the host cell [B1]
Host cell (ribosomes / enzymes) makes viral nucleic acid and proteins, which are assembled into new viruses. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 points.

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which binary fission in bacteria differs from mitosis in eukaryotic cells. (2)
hints: Think about the form of the DNA in a bacterium.
Does a bacterium have a nucleus or spindle?
questions.solution:
Binary fission involves circular DNA / no chromosomes or histones [B1]
No spindle (fibres) formed [B1]
No nucleus / nuclear envelope to break down [B1]
Plasmids are also replicated. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 differences.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to a bacterium's DNA and cytoplasm during binary fission. (2)
hints: There are two types of DNA in many bacteria.
How does the cell finally split?
questions.solution:
Circular DNA replicates (and plasmids replicate) [B1]
DNA loops move to opposite poles of the cell [B1]
Cytoplasm divides, producing two daughter cells (each with one copy of circular DNA and a variable number of plasmids). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 points.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil. Suggest two features of root hair cells that increase the rate of uptake, and explain how each feature does so. (2)
hints: Think about shape first.
Mineral ions are often taken up against a concentration gradient.
questions.solution:
Long thin extension, so large surface area [B1]
Many carrier proteins (in membrane), so more active transport of ions [B1]
Many mitochondria, so more ATP for active transport [B1]
Many aquaporins / channel proteins, so faster osmosis. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two features, each with a linked explanation (1 mark each).

questions.prompt: Cells lining kidney tubules reabsorb large volumes of water. Suggest two features of the cell-surface membranes of these cells that would increase the rate of water reabsorption, and explain each. (2)
hints: Water crosses membranes through special proteins.
Rate also depends on area.
questions.solution:
Many aquaporins / water channel proteins, so more water moves by osmosis [B1]
Folded membrane / microvilli, so large surface area [B1]
Thin / short diffusion distance (phospholipid bilayer). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two features, each with a linked explanation (1 mark each).

questions.prompt: Describe how sodium ions are involved in the absorption of glucose by epithelial cells of the ileum. (3)
hints: Start with what happens on the blood side of the cell.
Sodium ions are pumped out of the cell into the blood…
questions.solution:
Na⁺ actively transported out of the epithelial cell into the blood (by Na⁺/K⁺ pump, using ATP) [B1]
This keeps a low Na⁺ concentration inside the cell / maintains a Na⁺ gradient [B1]
Na⁺ diffuses into the cell from the lumen through a co-transporter protein [B1]
Carrying glucose with it, against the glucose concentration gradient [B1]
Glucose then moves into the blood by facilitated diffusion. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Na⁺ is actively pumped out of the cell into the blood, keeping the Na⁺ concentration in the cell low. Na⁺ then diffuses in from the lumen down its gradient through a co-transporter, carrying glucose with it against glucose's gradient. Glucose leaves into the blood by facilitated diffusion. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt: A carrier protein in the cell-surface membrane of stomach lining cells moves hydrogen ions out of the cell in exchange for potassium ions moving in. It uses ATP. Use your knowledge of active transport to suggest how this carrier protein moves the ions. (3)
hints: What happens to ATP, and what effect does that have on the protein?
Ions bind on one side and are released on the other.
questions.solution:
ATP is hydrolysed (to ADP + Pi), releasing energy / phosphorylating the carrier [B1]
This changes the shape (tertiary structure) of the carrier protein [B1]
H⁺ binds inside and is released outside; K⁺ binds outside and is released inside [B1]
Ions move against their concentration gradients. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: A respiratory inhibitor is added to cells lining the ileum. The rate of amino acid absorption decreases. Explain why. (3)
hints: What does a respiratory inhibitor reduce?
Amino acids are absorbed by co-transport with sodium ions.
questions.solution:
Less ATP produced [B1]
Less active transport of Na⁺ out of the cell (Na⁺/K⁺ pump) [B1]
So the Na⁺ concentration gradient (lumen → cell) is not maintained [B1]
So less co-transport of amino acids with Na⁺. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt:
A drug blocks the glucose co-transporter in the ileum. Scientists gave the drug to one group of mice and a placebo to a control group. The table shows their results. The difference between the groups is significant (P < 0.05).

The scientists concluded that the drug reduces glucose absorption. Use the data and your knowledge of water potential to explain why the results support this conclusion. (4)
hints: If glucose stays in the gut, what happens to the water potential of the gut contents?
What does P < 0.05 tell you?
questions.solution:
More glucose remains in the lumen (of the gut) [B1]
Lowers the water potential of the gut contents [B1]
So less water leaves the gut by osmosis / water moves into the gut by osmosis [B1]
Faeces water content higher in drug group and the difference is significant (P < 0.05) / unlikely to be due to chance. [B1]
questions.table:
Group | Water in faeces / %
Control (placebo) | 58
Drug | 72

questions.prompt: People who are lactose intolerant produce very little lactase. Explain why drinking milk can cause them to have diarrhoea (watery faeces). (4)
hints: Lactose is a disaccharide — can it be absorbed?
Think about the water potential of the gut contents.
questions.solution:
Lactose is not hydrolysed (to glucose and galactose) [B1]
Lactose cannot be absorbed (only monosaccharides are absorbed) [B1]
Lactose lowers the water potential of the gut contents / lumen [B1]
Water moves into the lumen by osmosis, so faeces contain more water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Cholera toxin causes chloride ion channels in ileum epithelial cells to stay open, so chloride ions move out of the cells into the lumen. Explain how this leads to severe, watery diarrhoea. (4)
hints: What happens to the water potential of the lumen?
Where does the water come from?
questions.solution:
Chloride ions move into the lumen [B1]
Water potential of the lumen decreases / becomes lower than in the cells [B1]
Water moves out of the epithelial cells into the lumen by osmosis [B1]
Water then moves from blood / tissue fluid into the cells, so large volumes are lost in faeces. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium. (3)
hints: How does the phagocyte recognise the bacterium?
Which organelle provides the enzymes?
questions.solution:
Phagocyte recognises foreign antigens / is attracted by chemicals [B1]
Engulfs the bacterium, forming a phagosome / vacuole [B1]
Lysosomes fuse with the phagosome [B1]
Lysozymes / hydrolytic enzymes digest / hydrolyse the bacterium. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe how a body cell infected with a virus is destroyed by the immune system. (3)
hints: How does the immune system know the cell is infected?
Which type of T cell kills infected cells?
questions.solution:
Infected cell presents viral antigens on its cell-surface membrane [B1]
Cytotoxic T cell with a complementary receptor binds to the antigen [B1]
T cell releases perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane [B1]
Cell becomes freely permeable / dies. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Explain how vaccination leads to long-term immunity against a disease. (3)
hints: What does a vaccine contain?
Which cells provide the long-term protection?
questions.solution:
Vaccine contains antigen (dead / weakened pathogen) [B1]
Triggers a primary immune response / B cells with complementary receptors activated and undergo clonal selection [B1]
Memory cells are produced [B1]
On reinfection, memory cells cause a faster, larger secondary response / more antibody before symptoms develop. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of helper T cells in the immune response. (3)
hints: What does a helper T cell bind to?
What chemical messengers do they release, and what do these stimulate?
questions.solution:
Receptor on helper T cell binds to complementary antigen on an antigen-presenting cell [B1]
Helper T cell is activated and divides by mitosis (clones) [B1]
Releases cytokines [B1]
Which stimulate B cells to divide / phagocytes / cytotoxic T cells. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the secondary immune response and explain why it is faster than the primary response. (3)
hints: Which cells remain after the first infection?
What do they quickly become?
questions.solution:
Memory B cells (remain in the blood from the primary response) [B1]
Recognise / bind the complementary antigen quickly [B1]
Divide rapidly by mitosis and differentiate into plasma cells [B1]
Produce large amounts of antibody quickly, so pathogen destroyed before symptoms. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of an antibody and explain how antibodies lead to the destruction of bacteria. (3)
hints: How many polypeptide chains does an antibody have?
What is agglutination?
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains (two heavy, two light) held by disulfide bridges [B1]
Variable region forms an antigen-binding site complementary to a specific antigen [B1]
Forms antigen–antibody complexes / causes agglutination (clumping) of bacteria [B1]
Clumped bacteria are engulfed by phagocytes. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: A virus has a surface protein with a similar shape to a protein on insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. Suggest how infection with this virus could lead to type 1 diabetes. (2)
hints: Antibodies bind to shapes.
What happens to the pancreatic cells?
questions.solution:
Antibodies / T cells made against the viral protein are also complementary to / bind the pancreatic cell protein [B1]
So the immune system destroys insulin-producing cells (so little insulin made). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a vaccine against one strain of influenza may not protect a person against a different strain. (2)
hints: What can change on the virus surface?
Will the memory cells still recognise it?
questions.solution:
Different strains have different (shaped) antigens / antigenic variability [B1]
Memory cells / antibodies from the vaccine are not complementary to the new antigen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Rheumatic fever can develop after a throat infection by streptococcal bacteria. Antibodies produced during the infection damage heart muscle. Suggest an explanation. (2)
hints: Compare the shapes of the bacterial antigen and a heart protein.
What do antibodies do when they bind?
questions.solution:
Bacterial antigen has a similar shape to a protein on heart cells [B1]
Antibodies are complementary to / bind heart cells, causing damage. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment
Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: Explain three features of the alveoli that make gas exchange efficient. (3)
hints: Fick's law: surface area, distance, gradient.
Give a feature and link it to one of those.
questions.solution:
Thin walls / one cell thick (squamous epithelium), so short diffusion distance [B1]
Many alveoli, so large surface area [B1]
Surrounded by a capillary network / ventilation, so a steep concentration gradient is maintained. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain three features of a leaf that make gas exchange efficient. (3)
hints: How do gases get into the leaf?
What is in the spongy mesophyll?
questions.solution:
Many stomata, so gases can enter / leave [B1]
Air spaces in spongy mesophyll, so gases diffuse quickly to cells [B1]
Thin leaf, so short diffusion distance [B1]
Large surface area of mesophyll cells for diffusion. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 features with explanation.

questions.prompt: Explain how an insect limits water loss while still exchanging gases. (3)
hints: What covers the insect's body?
How can the openings to the tracheal system be controlled?
questions.solution:
Spiracles can close (when less oxygen needed), reducing evaporation [B1]
Waxy cuticle, reducing evaporation from body surface [B1]
Hairs around spiracles trap moist air, reducing the water potential gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the counter-current mechanism makes gas exchange in fish gills efficient. (2)
hints: Which directions do blood and water flow?
What happens to the oxygen concentration gradient along the lamella?
questions.solution:
Blood and water flow in opposite directions [B1]
So a concentration gradient (of oxygen) is maintained along the whole length of the lamella / gill filament. [B1]

questions.prompt: Tuna are fast-swimming fish. They have a larger gill surface area per gram of body mass than slow-moving fish. Suggest why. (2)
hints: What is different about the metabolism of an active fish?
What does a larger surface area do?
questions.solution:
More active / higher (metabolic or respiratory) rate, so more oxygen needed [B1]
Larger surface area allows faster / more diffusion of oxygen. [B1]

questions.prompt: During flight, fluid at the ends of an insect's tracheoles is drawn into the muscle cells. Explain how this increases the rate of gas exchange. (2)
hints: Do gases diffuse faster in air or in water?
What is now in contact with more of the tracheole wall?
questions.solution:
Gases diffuse faster through air than through liquid [B1]
Larger surface area of tracheole wall exposed to air / more oxygen reaches muscle cells. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: Epithelial cells lining the ileum absorb glucose rapidly. Suggest two features of these cells that increase the rate of absorption, and explain how each feature does so. (2)
hints: One feature increases surface area.
Glucose absorption uses co-transport, which depends on ATP.
questions.solution:
Microvilli, so a large surface area (for carrier proteins / diffusion) [B1]
Many carrier / co-transporter proteins, so more glucose transported at once [B1]
Many mitochondria, so more ATP for active transport (of Na⁺ out of the cell). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two features, each with a linked explanation (1 mark each).

questions.prompt: Amylase is secreted into the lumen of the gut, but maltase is attached to the cell-surface membranes of epithelial cells in the ileum. Suggest an advantage of maltase being membrane-bound. (2)
hints: Where is glucose produced if the enzyme is on the membrane?
Think about what glucose has to reach to be absorbed.
questions.solution:
Glucose is produced close to the co-transporter / carrier proteins [B1]
So it is absorbed quickly / maintains a concentration gradient / is not lost or used by gut bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of membrane-bound disaccharidases in the ileum. (2)
hints: Name a disaccharide and its products.
Why does it matter that the products are small?
questions.solution:
Hydrolyse disaccharides (e.g. maltose / sucrose / lactose) into monosaccharides [B1]
Monosaccharides can then be absorbed (by co-transport / facilitated diffusion). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how endopeptidases and exopeptidases work together to digest proteins. (2)
hints: The prefixes endo- and exo- tell you where on the chain they act.
How does one enzyme help the other?
questions.solution:
Endopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds within the polypeptide / between amino acids in the middle [B1]
Exopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds at the ends, removing single amino acids / dipeptides [B1]
Endopeptidases create more ends for exopeptidases to act on. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of bile salts and lipase in the digestion of lipids. (2)
hints: Bile salts don't digest anything — what do they do to fat droplets?
What bonds does lipase break?
questions.solution:
Bile salts emulsify lipids into small droplets, increasing surface area (for lipase) [B1]
Lipase hydrolyses (ester bonds in) triglycerides into monoglycerides / glycerol and fatty acids. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: A person with a protein-deficient diet has a low concentration of protein in their blood plasma. Explain why tissue fluid accumulates in their body. (2)
hints: How does plasma protein affect water potential?
At which end of the capillary does water usually return?
questions.solution:
Water potential of plasma is higher / less negative [B1]
So less water returns to the capillary by osmosis (at the venule end). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a person with high blood pressure may produce more tissue fluid than normal. (2)
hints: What forces fluid out at the arteriole end of a capillary?
What happens if that force increases?
questions.solution:
Higher hydrostatic pressure (at the arteriole end of capillaries) [B1]
So more fluid / water and small molecules forced out of the capillaries. [B1]

questions.prompt: A parasite blocks the lymph vessels in a person's leg. Explain why the leg swells. (2)
hints: Not all tissue fluid returns to the capillaries.
Where does the excess normally go?
questions.solution:
Excess tissue fluid normally drains into the lymph vessels (and back to the blood) [B1]
If blocked, tissue fluid accumulates (in the tissues). [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: Name the two types of molecule that make up a chromosome in a eukaryotic cell. (1)
hints: Eukaryotic DNA is wound around something.
The answer includes a type of protein.
questions.solution: DNA and histones / (histone) proteins (both needed). [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Describe the role of transfer RNA (tRNA) in translation. (3)
hints: Each tRNA has two important regions — what is attached at each end?
Start with: each tRNA carries a specific amino acid…
questions.solution:
tRNA carries / binds a specific amino acid [B1]
Has an anticodon that is complementary to a codon on mRNA [B1]
Brings the amino acid to the ribosome (in the correct sequence) [B1]
Two tRNAs held at the ribosome so the amino acids can be joined by a peptide bond [B1]
tRNA is released (without its amino acid) and can collect another amino acid. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon. It brings its amino acid to the ribosome, where two tRNAs are held so their amino acids can be joined by a peptide bond. The tRNA is then released to collect another amino acid. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt: Describe how pre-mRNA is produced from a gene in a eukaryotic cell. Do not include splicing in your answer. (3)
hints: Think about what has to happen to the DNA double helix first.
Start with: hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands are broken…
questions.solution:
Hydrogen bonds between DNA strands broken / DNA helicase separates strands [B1]
Only one strand acts as a template [B1]
Free RNA nucleotides line up by complementary base pairing (uracil pairs with adenine) [B1]
RNA polymerase joins adjacent nucleotides [B1]
Forming phosphodiester bonds. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
DNA helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds so the strands separate; one strand is used as a template. Free RNA nucleotides align by complementary base pairing (U with A), and RNA polymerase joins them with phosphodiester bonds to form pre-mRNA. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt: Describe how a peptide bond is formed between two amino acids at a ribosome, and what then happens to the first tRNA molecule and the ribosome. (3)
hints: What type of reaction joins two monomers?
Which two groups on the amino acids react?
questions.solution:
Two tRNAs (with amino acids) are held at the ribosome [B1]
Condensation reaction (releasing water) [B1]
Between the amine group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of the other [B1]
Uses energy from ATP (hydrolysis) [B1]
First tRNA released and ribosome moves along mRNA to the next codon. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Two tRNAs bound to adjacent codons are held in the ribosome. A condensation reaction joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amine group of the other, using energy from ATP. The first tRNA is released and the ribosome moves one codon along the mRNA. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt:
A section of mRNA has the base sequence

A U G G C A U U C G A C

Give the base sequence of the DNA template strand it was transcribed from. (1)
hints: Use complementary base pairing.
In DNA, which base pairs with U on the RNA?
questions.solution:
T A C C G T A A G C T G [B1]

Model answer:
Pair each base: A→T, U→A, G→C, C→G.
DNA template: TAC CGT AAG CTG

questions.prompt:
Three mRNA codons are

C C A   G U U   A C G

Give the base sequences of the three tRNA anticodons that bind to these codons. (1)
hints: Anticodons are complementary to codons.
tRNA is RNA, so it contains U, not T.
questions.solution:
GGU  CAA  UGC [B1]

Model answer:
Complementary pairing (RNA to RNA): CCA→GGU, GUU→CAA, ACG→UGC.

questions.prompt:
A DNA template strand has the base sequence

T A C G G A C T T A A G

Give the base sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this strand. (1)
hints: mRNA is complementary to the template strand.
Remember A in DNA pairs with U in RNA.
questions.solution:
A U G C C U G A A U U C [B1]

Model answer:
T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C.
mRNA: AUG CCU GAA UUC

questions.prompt: Two different proteins are produced in a eukaryotic cell from the same gene. Explain how this is possible. (2)
hints: Think about what happens to pre-mRNA before translation.
Not every exon has to be kept.
questions.solution:
Pre-mRNA is spliced / introns removed [B1]
Different exons can be kept or removed (alternative splicing), giving different mRNA and so different amino acid sequences. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mRNA in a bacterium can be translated immediately after it is transcribed, whereas mRNA in a eukaryotic cell cannot. (2)
hints: What do eukaryotic genes contain that prokaryotic genes do not?
Where does translation happen relative to the DNA in each cell type?
questions.solution:
Prokaryotic genes do not contain introns, so no splicing is needed [B1]
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA must be spliced (introns removed) / leave the nucleus before translation. [B1]

questions.prompt: A eukaryotic gene is 3600 bases long. The polypeptide it codes for contains 450 amino acids. Use this information to explain why the gene contains far more bases than are needed to code for the polypeptide. (2)
hints: How many bases code for one amino acid?
questions.solution:
450 amino acids need only 1350 bases (+3 for the stop codon) / 3 bases per amino acid [B1]
The rest is non-coding DNA / introns, which are removed by splicing. [B1]

Model answer:
Each amino acid is coded for by a triplet, so 450 × 3 = 1350 bases (plus a stop codon). The remaining bases are introns / non-coding sequences, removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Explain how meiosis produces genetically different gametes. (4)
hints: There are two main processes.
One happens between homologous chromosomes in prophase I.
questions.solution:
Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes [B1]
Exchanges alleles / produces new combinations of alleles [B1]
Independent segregation of homologous chromosomes (in meiosis I) [B1]
Random arrangement on the equator, so gametes get different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between mitosis and meiosis. Explain why it is important that meiosis halves the chromosome number. (4)
hints: Compare number of divisions and the type of cells produced.
What happens when two gametes fuse?
questions.solution:
Meiosis has two divisions; mitosis has one [B1]
Meiosis produces haploid cells; mitosis produces diploid cells / meiosis produces genetically different cells; mitosis identical [B1]
Halving means fertilisation restores the diploid number [B1]
So the chromosome number stays constant from generation to generation. [B1]

Model answer:
2 differences (1 mark each) + 2 marks for the explanation.

questions.prompt:
A cell has a diploid number of 8.

(i) How many chromosomes are in each cell at the end of meiosis I, and how many chromatids does each chromosome have?
(ii) How many chromosomes are in each cell at the end of meiosis II, and how many chromatids does each chromosome have?
(iii) How many different combinations of chromosomes are possible in the gametes from independent segregation alone? (4)
hints: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates chromatids.
Number of combinations = 2ⁿ, where n is the haploid number.
questions.solution:
(i) 4 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids [B1]
(ii) 4 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid [B1]
(iii) 2⁴ [B1]
= 16. [B1]

Model answer:
(i) Homologous pairs separate → 4 chromosomes, each still 2 chromatids.
(ii) Chromatids separate → 4 chromosomes of 1 chromatid.
(iii) Haploid number 4 → 2⁴ = 16 combinations.

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Some bacteria secrete an enzyme called β-lactamase, which breaks down penicillin. Suggest and explain one advantage to the bacteria of secreting this enzyme into their surroundings. (2)
hints: Where does penicillin act — inside or at the surface of the bacterium?
What happens to bacteria that are not killed?
questions.solution:
Penicillin is broken down before it can reach / damage the cell wall [B1]
So the bacteria (and nearby bacteria) survive and reproduce / are resistant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Tuberculosis is treated with four different antibiotics taken together. Explain why using several antibiotics at once reduces the chance of antibiotic resistance developing. (3)
hints: How does resistance arise in the first place?
What is the chance of one bacterium being resistant to all four?
questions.solution:
Resistance arises by random mutation [B1]
A bacterium resistant to one antibiotic is (likely to be) killed by another [B1]
Very low probability of one bacterium having mutations for resistance to all the antibiotics [B1]
So resistant bacteria do not survive and reproduce / resistance allele frequency does not increase. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Explain why patients are told to complete the full course of antibiotics even when they feel better. (3)
hints: Which bacteria are left after a few days?
Use the language of natural selection.
questions.solution:
The most susceptible bacteria are killed first; some (more resistant) bacteria survive [B1]
If treatment stops, survivors reproduce [B1]
Passing on the resistance allele [B1]
So the frequency of resistance increases in the population. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Some farmers add antibiotics to animal feed. Explain how this could lead to human infections that are difficult to treat. (3)
hints: The antibiotic is a selection pressure.
How can resistance pass between different species of bacteria?
questions.solution:
A mutation gives some bacteria resistance [B1]
Antibiotic acts as a selection pressure — resistant bacteria survive and reproduce [B1]
Resistance allele frequency increases [B1]
Resistance (on plasmids) passed to other / pathogenic bacteria (horizontal transmission) that infect humans. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Using appearance, species P and Q were placed in the same genus and species R in a different genus. Later DNA comparisons showed that R and Q have more similar base sequences than P and Q. Suggest what this shows about the evolutionary relationships of these species. (2)
hints: Which pair shares the most recent common ancestor?
Why might P and Q look alike if they aren't closest relatives?
questions.solution:
R and Q are most closely related / share the most recent common ancestor [B1]
Similar appearance of P and Q is due to similar environments / convergent evolution, not close relationship. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why classification based on DNA base sequences is more reliable than classification based on observable features. (2)
hints: What can affect observable features apart from genes?
What does DNA directly show?
questions.solution:
Observable features can be affected by the environment / similar features can evolve separately (convergent evolution) [B1]
DNA base sequence directly reflects genetic relatedness / more differences can be compared. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two populations of birds look very different but can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Suggest what this tells you about their classification, and explain why they look different. (2)
hints: What is the definition of a species?
What causes variation within a species?
questions.solution:
They are the same species (able to produce fertile offspring) [B1]
Differences due to (genetic) variation within the species / different alleles / environment. [B1]

questions.prompt: List the eight taxonomic ranks in order, starting with domain. (1)
hints: There are eight ranks in the hierarchy.
A common mnemonic is 'Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.
questions.solution: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The grey wolf is classified as follows: Domain Eukarya, Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order ________, Family Canidae, Genus ________, Species lupus.

Complete the two missing names. (1)
hints: Wolves are meat-eating mammals.
The genus is the first word of the binomial name for the dog family.
questions.solution: Carnivora and Canis (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the three domains used to classify living organisms. (1)
hints: One contains all organisms with a nucleus.
Prokaryotes are split into two domains.
questions.solution: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya (all three needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: The domestic cat is Felis catus and the wildcat is Felis silvestris. Name the lowest taxon that both species belong to. (1)
hints: Look at the first word of each name.
The first word of a binomial is…
questions.solution: Genus. [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant was renamed from Aster novae-angliae to Symphyotrichum novae-angliae. Which taxon was changed? (1)
hints: Which part of the name changed?
The first part of a binomial name refers to…
questions.solution: Genus. [B1]

questions.prompt: What do the two parts of a binomial name represent? (1)
hints: The first part is capitalised.
The second part is not.
questions.solution: Genus (first part) and species (second part). [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Explain why comparing DNA base sequences can give more information about relationships than comparing the amino acid sequences of proteins. (3)
hints: Is the genetic code degenerate?
Does all DNA code for amino acids?
questions.solution:
Genetic code is degenerate — different triplets can code for the same amino acid [B1]
So some base changes / mutations do not change the amino acid sequence but are detected in DNA [B1]
Non-coding DNA / introns can also be compared. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how comparing the amino acid sequence of a protein can be used to find out how closely related two species are. (3)
hints: The same protein must be compared.
What do fewer differences suggest?
questions.solution:
Use the same protein from both species [B1]
Determine / compare the sequence of amino acids [B1]
Count the number of differences [B1]
Fewer differences = more closely related / more recent common ancestor. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe how immunological comparisons can be used to find out how closely related two species are. (3)
hints: Antibodies are made against a protein from one species.
What is measured when they are mixed with another species' protein?
questions.solution:
Protein from species A injected into an animal (e.g. rabbit), which makes antibodies against it [B1]
Serum / antibodies mixed with the same protein from species B [B1]
Amount of precipitate / antibody binding measured [B1]
More precipitate = more similar protein = more closely related. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

category: Energy transfers in and between organisms
Energy transfers in and between organisms

questions.prompt: A germinating seed contains a store of starch. Suggest how this starch provides energy for the growing seedling. (2)
hints: Starch is too large to be used directly — what must happen to it?
What process releases energy from glucose?
questions.solution:
Starch is hydrolysed (by amylase) to maltose / glucose [B1]
Glucose is used in respiration to produce ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how triglycerides stored in adipose tissue provide energy for muscle cells. (2)
hints: What enzyme breaks down triglycerides?
What are the products?
questions.solution:
Triglycerides hydrolysed (by lipase) into glycerol and fatty acids [B1]
These are respired / used in respiration to produce ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Muscle cells store glycogen. Explain how this glycogen provides energy for muscle contraction during exercise. (2)
hints: Two steps: break the store down, then make the energy currency.
What is the immediate energy source for contraction?
questions.solution:
Glycogen hydrolysed to glucose [B1]
Glucose respired (aerobically or anaerobically) producing ATP, which is hydrolysed to release energy for contraction. [B1]

category: Energy transfers in and between organisms
Energy transfers in and between organisms

questions.prompt: Saprobiotic fungi secrete cellulase onto dead plant material. Suggest and explain one advantage to the fungus of secreting this enzyme rather than taking in whole pieces of plant material. (2)
hints: Can cellulose cross a cell membrane?
What do the products of digestion do next?
questions.solution:
Cellulose is too large to be absorbed / cross the membrane [B1]
Enzyme hydrolyses it to glucose (small, soluble), which can be absorbed and used in respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The first division of a zygote takes 30 hours. Each division after that takes 11 hours. After 96 hours the embryo has a total volume of 4.48 × 10⁻³ mm³.

Calculate the mean volume of one cell after 96 hours. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: Work out how many divisions fit into 96 hours.
96 − 30 = 66 hours for later divisions; each division doubles cell number.
questions.solution:
Number of cells = 2⁷ = 128 [M1]
Mean volume = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³. [A1]

Model answer:
Later divisions: (96 − 30) ÷ 11 = 6, so 7 divisions in total.
Cells = 2⁷ = 128.
Mean volume = 4.48 × 10⁻³ ÷ 128 = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³.

questions.prompt:
A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Each bacterium has a volume of 1.5 µm³.

Starting with a single bacterium, calculate the total volume of all the bacteria after 4 hours. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: How many 20-minute periods are there in 4 hours?
Number of cells = 2ⁿ.
questions.solution:
2¹² = 4096 bacteria [M1]
Total volume = 6.1 × 10³ µm³ (accept 6.144 × 10³). [A1]

Model answer:
4 hours = 240 min → 240 ÷ 20 = 12 divisions.
2¹² = 4096 cells.
4096 × 1.5 = 6144 µm³ = 6.1 × 10³ µm³.

questions.prompt:
A culture contains 5.0 × 10³ animal cells. Every cell divides by mitosis once every 6 hours.

Calculate the number of cells after 2 days. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: How many 6-hour cycles in 48 hours?
Multiply the starting number by 2 for each cycle.
questions.solution:
8 divisions / ×256 [M1]
1.28 × 10⁶ cells. [A1]

Model answer:
48 ÷ 6 = 8 divisions → 2⁸ = 256.
5.0 × 10³ × 256 = 1.28 × 10⁶ cells.

questions.prompt:
A rat with a mass of 250 g is given an antibiotic at a dose of 40 mg kg⁻¹ day⁻¹ for 5 days.

Calculate the total mass of antibiotic given. (2)
hints: Convert the rat's mass into kg first.
Daily dose × number of days.
questions.solution:
Daily dose = 0.25 × 40 = 10 mg [M1]
Total = 50 mg. [A1]

Model answer:
250 g = 0.25 kg.
Daily dose = 0.25 × 40 = 10 mg.
Total = 10 × 5 = 50 mg.

questions.prompt:
A patient with a mass of 75 kg needs a single dose of antibiotic of 10 mg kg⁻¹. The antibiotic is supplied as 250 mg tablets.

Calculate how many tablets the patient should take. (2)
hints: Find the total mass needed first.
Then divide by the mass per tablet.
questions.solution:
Dose = 750 mg [M1]
3 tablets. [A1]

Model answer:
75 × 10 = 750 mg; 750 ÷ 250 = 3 tablets.

questions.prompt:
A mouse with a mass of 18 g is given a drug at a dose of 12 mg kg⁻¹.

Calculate the mass of drug given. Give your answer in µg. (2)
hints: Convert g to kg.

questions.prompt:
The number of bacteria in two groups of mice was recorded as log₁₀ values. Group X: 6.2. Group Y: 4.8.

Calculate the percentage by which the number of bacteria in group Y is lower than in group X. (2)
hints: Convert each value: number = 10^(log value).
Percentage decrease = (X − Y) ÷ X × 100.

questions.prompt:
In a culture, log₁₀ (number of bacteria) fell from 7.5 to 7.2 after an antibiotic was added.

Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of bacteria. (2)
hints: Convert both log values into actual numbers.

questions.prompt:
Over 24 hours, log₁₀ (number of bacteria) in a culture increased from 3.0 to 5.5.

Calculate how many times larger the population was after 24 hours. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2)
hints: Convert both values, then divide.

questions.prompt:
A student measured a rectangular leaf section. Length = 4.25 ± 0.15 cm. Width = 2.10 ± 0.08 cm.

Calculate the area of the section to an appropriate number of significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
hints: Area = length × width; give it to the same number of s.f. as the data.
Percentage uncertainties add when you multiply.

questions.prompt:
A cell seen under a microscope is approximately rectangular. Length = 48 ± 2 µm. Width = 22 ± 2 µm.

Calculate the area of the cell to an appropriate number of significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
hints: The data are given to 2 s.f.
Add the two percentage uncertainties.
questions.solution:
Area = 1.1 × 10³ µm² (2 s.f.) [M1]
% uncertainties: 4.2% and 9.1% [M1]
Total percentage uncertainty = 13%. [A1]

Model answer:
Area = 48 × 22 = 1056 → 1.1 × 10³ µm² (2 s.f.).
2 ÷ 48 × 100 = 4.17%; 2 ÷ 22 × 100 = 9.09%.
Total = 13.3% ≈ 13%.

questions.prompt:
An agar cube has sides of 1.50 ± 0.05 cm.

Calculate the volume of the cube to an appropriate number of significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
hints: Volume = side³.
When a quantity is cubed, its percentage uncertainty is multiplied by 3.
questions.solution:
Volume = 3.38 cm³ (3 s.f.) [M1]
% uncertainty of side = 3.3% [M1]
Volume percentage uncertainty = 10%. [A1]

Model answer:
V = 1.50³ = 3.375 → 3.38 cm³.
0.05 ÷ 1.50 × 100 = 3.33%; × 3 = 10%.

questions.prompt:
A student's drawing of a cell is 50 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 25 µm.

Calculate the magnification of the drawing, and state what should be added to the drawing to show its size. (2)
hints: Convert both lengths to the same unit.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
questions.solution:
× 2000 [M1]
Scale bar / the magnification. [A1]

Model answer:
50 mm = 50 000 µm. 50 000 ÷ 25 = × 2000. Add a scale bar (or state the magnification).

questions.prompt:
Scientists tested herbicide X on barley (a crop) and fat hen (a weed). Leaf discs were placed in water or herbicide X, and ion leakage from the cells was measured (arbitrary units). Ion leakage shows membrane damage. A difference between two means greater than the least significant difference (LSD) is significant.

Evaluate the use of herbicide X to control fat hen in a barley crop. (4)
hints: Compare each difference with its LSD.
Then think about the limitations of the method.
questions.solution:
Fat hen leakage increased by 47, greater than its LSD of 9, so significant membrane damage [B1]
Barley increased by 6, less than its LSD of 8, so not significant / barley not damaged [B1]
Limitation: leaf discs / lab conditions, not whole plants in a field [B1]
Limitation: only one concentration / only membrane damage measured, not plant death or crop yield / only one weed species. [B1]
questions.table:
Plant | Leakage in water | Leakage in X | LSD
Barley | 12 | 18 | 8
Fat hen | 14 | 61 | 9

questions.prompt:
A company claimed that mouthwash A kills bacteria better than mouthwash B. Paper discs soaked in each mouthwash were placed on agar plates of one species of mouth bacterium. The table shows the mean diameter of the clear zones around the discs, ± standard deviation.

Evaluate the company's claim. (4)
hints: Work out mean ± 1 SD for each — do the ranges overlap?
Is a lab test on one species the same as use in a mouth?
questions.solution:
A has the larger mean clear zone (18 vs 15 mm) [B1]
But ± SD ranges overlap (16.5–19.5 and 11–19), so difference may not be significant / a statistical test is needed [B1]
B more variable (larger SD), so less reliable [B1]
Only one species tested / agar not the same as conditions in the mouth / concentration and contact time may differ. [B1]
questions.table:

questions.prompt:
In a trial, 40 patients with high blood pressure took a new drug and 40 took a placebo for 8 weeks. Mean systolic blood pressure fell by 12 mmHg in the drug group and by 4 mmHg in the placebo group. A statistical test gave P = 0.08.

Evaluate the claim that the drug lowers blood pressure. (4)
hints: What does P = 0.08 mean compared with 0.05?
Think about trial design — good features and limitations.
questions.solution:
Drug group had a larger fall in blood pressure [B1]
But P > 0.05, so difference not significant / could be due to chance [B1]
Placebo group is a valid control (good design) [B1]
Small sample / short trial / no information on side effects, dose, or whether double-blind. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would collect and analyse data to find out whether there is a significant difference in the mean shell length of limpets on an exposed rocky shore and on a sheltered rocky shore. (5)
hints: How do you avoid bias when choosing limpets?
Which statistical test compares two means?
questions.solution:
Random sampling, e.g. random coordinates from a grid / random number generator [B1]
Large sample (e.g. at least 30) on each shore [B1]
Measure shell length with callipers / ruler [B1]
Calculate mean (and standard deviation) for each shore [B1]
Use a Student's t-test [B1]
Null hypothesis of no difference; compare with critical value at P = 0.05. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

Any 5 points.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would collect and analyse data to find out whether there is a correlation between light intensity and the number of daisy plants across a field next to a woodland. (5)
hints: Light changes from the woodland edge into the field — how would you sample along that?
Which test is used for correlation?
questions.solution:
Use a transect (line) from woodland into the field [B1]
Place quadrats at regular intervals along it [B1]
Count daisies in each quadrat [B1]
Measure light intensity at each quadrat with a light meter [B1]
Use Spearman's rank correlation coefficient [B1]
Null hypothesis of no correlation; compare with critical value at P = 0.05. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

Model answer:
Any 5 points.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would collect and analyse data to find out whether the distribution of two snail species is associated with habitat (woodland or grassland). (5)
hints: You are counting categories, not measuring.
Which test looks for an association between categories?
questions.solution:
Random quadrats / sampling in each habitat [B1]
Same number / size of quadrats in each habitat [B1]
Count the number of each snail species in each habitat [B1]
Use a chi-squared test (contingency table) comparing observed and expected frequencies [B1]
Null hypothesis of no association; compare with critical value at P = 0.05 with correct degrees of freedom. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student used a respirometer containing soda lime to measure oxygen uptake by germinating seeds. Suggest why the apparatus was left in a water bath for 10 minutes before readings were taken, and why soda lime was used. (2)
